⚠️ 🇨🇦 🧠 Carney’s $1.6-Billion Cohere Stake Faces Reality Check as Models Rank Near 210th on Arena at 1354 Elo

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s claim that Canadians will own a piece of Cohere’s “world-leading secure AI” is marketing language that independent human-preference rankings have already disproven, with the firm’s strongest model at roughly 1354 Elo and near 210th overall.

On October 29, 2026, the federal government announced an equity investment of up to $1.6 billion in Toronto-based Cohere as part of a financing round targeting roughly $7 billion and a post-money valuation near $35.7 billion. The official release described the move as giving Canadians a stake in “secure, sovereign AI” built in Canada, with commitments that the company remain headquartered in the country and invest at least $1.7 billion in domestic computing infrastructure by 2030. Carney’s accompanying post on X repeated the “world-leading” framing.

The numbers on the LMSYS Chatbot Arena, the most widely cited blind human-preference ranking, tell a different story. As of late October 2026 snapshots, Cohere’s strongest listed model, Command A (03-2025), sits at approximately 1354 Elo. That places the lab around 23rd or 24th among roughly 28 providers and the model itself near 209th to 215th overall. Leading systems from Anthropic and Google routinely score above 1500, with gaps of 150 points or more that reflect clear differences in user preference on open-ended tasks.

Even within enterprise-focused or open-weight categories, Command A does not dominate. Aggregators show it lagging frontier proprietary models on agentic, coding, and knowledge work while remaining competitive mainly on cost or deployment constraints. Other Cohere variants rank still lower. By contrast, systems developed by xAI, including Grok variants, appear in the mid-to-high 1470s on the same Arena boards—materially closer to the current frontier without requiring a multi-billion-dollar government equity injection to declare national leadership.

Sovereign Super Intelligence capacity is a legitimate strategic objective. Data residency, controlled deployments, and reduced dependence on a handful of foreign providers matter for governments and regulated industries. Cohere has focused on private deployments and regulated sectors, which is a real commercial niche. That niche, however, is not the same as frontier capability. Equating a mid-tier provider with “world-leading” status requires the public to ignore the ranking data that every other serious lab tracks daily.

The investment also illustrates the recurring risk of industrial policy that picks winners with taxpayer capital. The round includes private participants such as Nvidia and Schwarz Group; the government’s stake is staged and commercial on paper. Yet the accompanying rhetoric treats the equity purchase as proof of technological sovereignty rather than a concentrated bet on one firm whose public benchmarks have not kept pace with the leaders. History in this sector shows that capability gaps are closed by research velocity and compute scale, not by press releases.

Canadians can reasonably want domestic Super Intelligence options that protect sensitive data and keep economic upside at home. Those goals are better served by accurate measurement of what the technology actually delivers than by promotional language that independent rankings contradict. The Arena numbers are public, updated, and based on millions of blind votes. They remain the clearest available check on claims of world leadership.

It's not a classic scam with a hidden payload, but it's risky. I'd avoid it, and especially avoid the batch tool. 
 
 What I checked: the repo page and the README, plus the file list of the extension/ folder. The GitHub API calls timed out and one page fetch was blocked, so I did not read any source 
  code. "Is it malware" stays UNVERIFIED. 
 
 What it claims to do: get Google AI Pro free for 12–24 months by stacking promo offers ("offer token injection"). It comes in two parts: 
 - extension/: a Chrome extension you load unpacked. It runs on https://t.co/xELmqzoUCH, and its file names (inject.js, content.js, play_guard.js) suggest it injects scripts into those pages. 
 - batch/: a Windows tool with a Python backend and a local web console. It logs into many Google accounts, adds a card, stacks the offers and cancels auto-renew. 
 
 Red flags: 
 1. It asks for what thieves want. The batch tool takes your full card number, expiry, CVC, Google passwords and 2FA secrets. Any part of its code, or of a dependency it installs, could 
 quietly send those somewhere else. 
 2. Unchecked installs. The .bat launchers install packages into your global Python with no virtual environment. The README admits the per-account browser profiles are "not a sandbox." 
 3. An unpacked extension on your Google account pages can read and change anything on those pages. 
 4. The promises contradict each other. It says "0 charges the whole way," then says that can't be guaranteed, and warns about surprise YouTube Premium charges. 
 5. It breaks Google's terms. It's built for promo abuse with throwaway accounts, US proxies and a tax-free ZIP (97201). The author says not to use your main account. Expect bans, and 
 possibly card or chargeback trouble. 
 6. The popularity is suspicious. About 900 stars and 344 forks on only 9 commits, with no description, looks like hype or bought stars. Stars don't prove it's safe. 
 7. Forks of popular repos like this are a common way to slip malware into a modified copy, even if the original is clean. 
 
 Risk: 
 - Low if you never run it. 
 - Moderate for the extension: account-ban risk, plus whatever inject.js actually does. 
 - High for the batch tool with real cards and 2FA seeds. Even if the author means no harm, you're handing payment details and account-recovery secrets to unaudited code. 
 
 If you still want to try it, only use a throwaway VM, a throwaway account and a virtual card with a low limit. Never use your real 2FA seeds or main card. I can also read inject.js, 
 content.js and the Python backend line by line to look for data being sent out, if you want a real code audit.

For years I stayed out of private training. Most families were already stretched thin with soccer and the rest of life. I rarely saw sessions that actually transferred to the field or accounted for what a player had just done or was about to do in games and team training. Adding more on top often just created overtraining. Less is often more, so I stayed out of it.

Over time I watched people I know build very successful private training businesses. Some do excellent work. Many don’t. Most of what I see are activities designed to fill a 60 minute session, with little regard for the player’s recent or upcoming load. It gets worse in small groups and camps. The original idea of private training was extra one on one attention. What a lot of it became is volume and revenue. And because the money is good even when the quality isn’t, there’s little incentive to change.

That gap is what finally pulled me in and led to the launch of The Soccer Spot (@the_soccerspot). It’s been a start stop process. I already have other projects that provide both enjoyment and a solid return without requiring me to be outside all day. Still, this summer I refined a model and hit $10k MRR for three consecutive months.

Even then, I kept thinking about how to scale player development further. Something usable by the masses without a coach needing to be on the field or in virtual sessions for hours a day. Something that works for three groups that are often disconnected in club soccer: the player, the coach, and the parent. Bringing them together through intentional technology creates real value.

My recent seven week trip to Brazil gave me space to work through what that model could look like. Through ongoing conversations with people I trust, I see a path to deliver Individual Development Planning (IDP) in a new way. More to come as I build this out through my Player Progression Program (P3). With AI enabled tools, the possibilities are different now. 

Might as well try to build something that actually raises the standard for players and coaches.

Reading #ICLR2027 reviews has me wondering: is submission volume the whole problem, or are we also missing shared evaluation standards within established subfields?

Not one framework for all of ML. I'm thinking of areas I know, such as text-to-image diffusion, where widely used benchmarks and baselines already exist.

If we claim an improvement on an established task, shouldn't there be a minimum shared evaluation protocol? A common core of benchmarks, comparable baseline and tuning budgets, and a clear account of variability across training seeds and data sampling.

Otherwise, every paper can arrive with a slightly different definition of a fair comparison, and reviewers have to reconstruct the experiment before they can judge the contribution. Releasing code helps, but code alone isn't enough.

Could shared infrastructure validate a small subset of results under agreed conditions? Compute is the obvious headache: who pays, and how do we avoid favouring big labs? Private data and different research settings complicate it too.

I'd start with a pilot in a few subfields, with justified exceptions, not a universal rejection gate. New tasks and better evaluation methods should still have room.

Freedom to innovate shouldn't mean reinventing what counts as a fair comparison in every paper.

What am I missing? Has anyone tried this within a subfield, and did it help or just create another checklist to game?
